Paleomagnetism of the Late Cretaceous ignimbrite from the
Okhotsk-Chukotka Volcanic Belt, Kolyma-Omolon Composite
Terrane: Tectonic implications
Yo-ichiro Otofujia,∗, Haider Zamanb, Gen Shogakia, Hanae Sekia, Vladimir F. Polinc,
Daisuke Miurad, Hyeon-Seon Ahna, Yurii Ivanove, Porel Minyuke, Peter Ziminf
aDepartment of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Faculty of Science, Kobe University, Kobe, Japan
bDepartment of Geology, Faculty of Science, Taibah University, Madinah 41477, Saudi Arabia
cRussian Academy of Science, Far East Geological Institute, Vladivostok, Russia
dAbiko Research Laboratory, CRIEPI, 1646 Abiko, Chiba, Japan
eRussian Academy of Science, North-East Interdisciplinary Scientific Research Institute, Portovaya 16, Magadan, Russia
fRussian Academy of Science, Pacific Oceanological Institute, Vladivostok, Russia

Keywords:
Tectonics

Eurasia

Kolyma-Omolon-Chukotka
a
Block
b s t r a c t
New Late Cretaceous paleomagnetic results from the Okhotsk-Chukotka Volcanic Belt in the Kolyma-
Omolon Composite Terrane yield stable and consistent remanent directions. The Late Cretaceous
(86–81 Ma) ignimbrites from the Kholchan and Ola suites were sampled at 19 sites in the Magadan area
(60.4◦N, 151.0◦E). We isolated the characteristic paleomagnetic directions from 16 sampled sites using
an alternating field demagnetization procedure. The primary nature of these directions is ascertained
by dual polarities and positive fold tests. A tilt-corrected mean direction (D = 42.8◦, I = 84.7◦, k = 46.0,
˛ 95= 10.0◦) yields a paleomagnetic pole of 66.7◦N, 168.5◦E (A95= 18.8◦) which appears almost identi-
cal to the 90–67 Ma pole reported from the Lake El’gygytgyn area of the Okhotsk-Chukotka Volcanic
Belt (Chukotka Terrane). This consistency suggests that the Kolyma-Omolon Composite Terrane and
Chukotka Terrane has acted as a single tectonic unit since 80 Ma without any significant internal defor-
mation. Accordingly, we calculate a combined 80 Ma characteristic paleomagnetic pole (Long. = 164.7◦E,
Lat. = 68.0◦, A95= 10.9◦, N = 12) for the Kolyma-Omolon-Chukotka Block which falls 16.5–17.5◦south of the
same age poles from Europe and East Asia. We ascribe this discrepancy in pole positions to tectonic activ-
ity in the area and infer a southward displacement of 1640 ± 1380 km for the Kolyma-Omolon-Chukotka
Block with respect to the North American and Eurasian blocks since 80 Ma; more than 260 km of it is
attributed to tectonic displacement in the Arctic Ocean due to the opening of the Canadian Basin.
© 2015 Elsevier Ltd. All rights reserved.
1. Introduction
The present-day Eurasian Continent is a collage of several con-
tinental blocks formed as a consequences of sequential collisions
and suturing. As shown in Fig. 1, the northeastern part of this
mega continent comprises the Siberian Craton, Kolyma-Omolon
∗ Corresponding author. Tel.: +81 78 803 5730; fax: +81 8 78 803 5757.
E-mail addresses: otofuji@kobe-u.ac.jp (Y.-i. Otofuji),

(V.F. Polin), dmiura@criepi.denken.or.jp (D. Miura), 101s429s@stu.kobe-u.ac.jp
(H.-S. Ahn), minyuk@neisri.ru (Y. Ivanov), pal105@neisri.ru (P. Minyuk),
petr.zimin.poi92@mail.ru (P.
Composite
Zimin).
Terrane and Chukotka Terrane (Parfenov et al., 2009;
Stone et al., 2009). Amalgamation of the Kolyma-Omolon Com-
posite Terrane with Siberia in the Mesozoic has been described as
one of the paramount tectonic events in the northeastern part of
Eurasia (Parfenov et al., 2009). A boundary between the Kolyma-
Omolon Composite Terrane and the Siberian Craton is characterized
by prominent topographic features including the 1000 km long “S”
shaped Verkhoyansk mountain range and the 1500 km long convex
Chersky mountain range. These topographic expressions are analo-
gous to those developed along the India-Asia and NCB-SCB collision
zones. Thorough understanding at the scale of the Kolyma-Omolon
Composite Terrane is required to elucidate collision tectonics in the
northeastern part of Eurasia.
The Okhotsk-Chukotka Volcanic Belt (OCVB) of northeastern
Eurasia, which is considered to be one of the largest volcanic
http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.jog.2015.03.003
0264-3707/© 2015 Elsevier Ltd. All rights reserved.

### page_2
2 Y.-i. Otofuji et al. / Journal of Geodynamics 91 (2015) 1–12
Fig. 1. (a) A simplified tectono-geographical map of the Arctic region. (b) Structural sketch map of the Kolyma-Omolon Composite Terrane and Chukotka Terrane (modified
from Stone et al., 2009).
provinces in the world, extends from the Chukotka Terrane in the
northeast via Kolyma-Omolon Composite Terrane to the Verhoy-
ansk mountain range. According to some of the recent geological
studies (Hourigan and Akinin, 2004; Belyi, 2008; Stone et al., 2009;
Sakhno et al., 2010), this belt was formed as a consequences of late
Cretaceous volcanic activities. Until a few years ago, some geolo-
gists believed that the OCVB is a subduction related belt (Hourigan
and Akinin, 2004; Parfenov et al., 2009; Akinin and Miller, 2011).
However, Tikhomirov et al. (2012) recently attributed it to silicic
igneous province formed in the intra-plate environment. Although
the origin of volcanism in this belt remains uncertain, their paleo-
magnetic signatures can help us to document the Late Mesozoic
paleo-geographic framework of the Kolyma-Omolon Composite
Terrane and the Chukotka Terrane.
Accordingly this paper presents new paleomagnetic data from
the Kolyma-Omolon Composite Terrane because paleomagnetism
can provides a quantitative record of block rotation and N-
S displacement (Fig. 1). For this purpose we sampled volcanic
rocks exposed in the Magadan area (60.4◦N, 151.0◦E) of the
OCVB.
2. Geologic setting
As described by Parfenov et al. (2009) the northeastern part of
Eurasia (east of the Siberian Craton) is made up of several terranes;
the Verkhoyansk fold and thrust belt, Kolyma-Omolon Compos-
ite Terrane, Chukotka Terrane and Koryak-Kamchatka
accretionary
Cenozoic
belt (Fig. 1). These terranes were amalgamated as a
result of sequential collisions and accretions during the Mesozoic
and Cenozoic. Formation of the Mesozoic Verkhoyansk fold and
thrust belt, as a result of the collision of the Siberian Craton with the
allochthonous Kolyma-Omolon Composite Terrane, was followed
by the Chukotka Terrane accretion (Oxman, 2003). An extensive
intra-plate magmatic activity from the Early to Late Cretaceous
(from 106 ± 1.7 to 74 ± 1.2 Ma), which brought widespread volcanic
emplacement over the Mesozoic assemblages of the Kolyma-
Omolon and Chukotka terranes, has been considered to be the
cause of OCVB formation (Tikhomirov et al., 2012). The Cenozoic
Koryak-Kamchatka accretionary belt formed as a final phase of this
sequence.
The Arman volcanic field in the Magadan area forms the cen-
tral part of the Okhotsk sector in the OCVB (Hourigan and Akinin,
2004). These volcanics were emplaced over deformed sedimentary
rocks of the Momoltykich and Khasyn suites deposited in a pas-
sive margin back-arc basin (marine environment) from the Permian
to the Jurassic. As shown in Fig. 2, the Arman volcanic field is
divided into six suites; the Arman, Narauli, Kholchan, Ulyn, Ola
and Mygdykit in ascending order (Anorov et al., 2013a,b). Based
on floral assemblages (the Arman flora) found in the type area late
Albian and Cenomanian ages have been assigned to the Arman vol-
canic field. The40Ar/39Ar dating assigns an age of 85.5–85.6 Ma to
the Narauli Suite, 81.7–83.6 Ma to the Ola Suite and 74.0–78.8 Ma
to the Mygdykit Suite. Hence, Late Cretaceous age is assigned to the
Arman volcanic field.

### page_3
Y.-i. Otofuji et al. / Journal of Geodynamics 91 (2015) 1–12 3
Fig. 2. Geological map of the study area (Magadan), a part of the Arman volcanic field in the OCVB (modified from Anorov et al., 2013a,b). Lithostratigraphic columns are
also shown together with40Ar/39Ar ages (Hourigan and Akinin, 2004). Sampling sites are shown by closed circles. A–F: sampling localities.
The volcanic rocks of the Kholchan and Ola suites which
yields 40Ar/39Ar ages of 81–86 Ma were sampled at 19 sites for
this paleomagnetic study (Fig. 2). The Kholchan suite consists of
rhyolite-dacite tuffs, welded tuffs and volcanic flows with local
lenses of tuffaceous sandstones, conglomerate and siltstones. Con-
versely, the Ola suite consists of non-welded to moderately welded
ash-flow tuffs and tabular flows of crystal rich rhyolite. The sam-
pled sites are located near the Agan Caldera, on the north side of
the city of Magadan (60.4◦N, 151.0◦E). Approximately 8–11 pale-
omagnetic block samples, from 3 to 14 m in covered area, were
collected at each site. Orientation of each sample was made by
magnetic compass, because a lack of sunshine in the study area
prevented us from using a sun-compass. Bedding attitude at each
sampling site was measured using the eutaxitic structure of the vol-
canic rocks (stretched pumice lineation and aligned phenocrysts).
Because an eutaxitic structure cannot always indicate a paleohori-
zontal plane, samples were collected from widely spaced outcrops
to reduce the expected error from uncertain tectonic correction.
The present day geomagnetic field declination at each sampling site
was noted from International Geomagnetic Reference Field (IGRF)
(the International Association of Geomagnetism and Aeronomy
Working Group V-MOD, 2010).
3. Laboratory procedures
Cylindrical specimens of 25 mm in diameter and 22 mm
in length were prepared from each block sample in the
laboratory. Natural remanent magnetizations (NRMs) were mea-
sured using the Kobe University based spinner magnetometer
(Natsuhara Giken SMM-85). One specimen per sample was
subjected to stepwise thermal demagnetization (ThD) up to
620◦C using a “Natsuhara Giken TDE-91C” thermal demagnetizer
with a residual field of less than 5nT. To obtain
paleomagnetic
reliable
results, duplicate specimens were demagnetized
by alternating field demagnetization (AFD) using a “Natsuhara
Giken DEM93” AF demagnetizer. Demagnetization results were
plotted on orthogonal vector diagrams (Zijderveld, 1967) to
assess component structure and on equal-area projections
to evaluate directional stability during demagnetizations. The
remanent directions were identified using principal compo-
nent analysis (Kirschvink, 1980) and the great circle method
(Halls, 1978; McFadden and McElhinny, 1988). Site-mean
directions were calculated using Fisherian (Fisher, 1953) and
McFadden and McElhinny statistics (McFadden and McElhinny,
1988).
4. Results
4.1. Rock magnetism
Samples from five ignimbrite layers corresponding to sites
MA01, MA02, MA05, MA10 and MA16 were analyzed for rock
magnetic characteristics. Progressive acquisition of isothermal
remanent magnetization (IRM) was performed on representa-
tive specimens up to a maximum field of 2.0 T using a Magnetic
Measurements Pulse Magnetizer (MMPM-10). Thermal demagne-
tization of the composite IRMs (imparted at 2.0 T, 0.4 T and 0.12 T
along the z, y and x axes of the specimens, respectively) was
conducted to detect the unblocking temperature spectra of the ana-
lyzed specimens (Lowrie, 1990). The IRM acquisition curves (Fig. 3)
show complete saturation up to a 0.3 T applied field yielding mag-
netite as a dominant remanence carrier. Thermal demagnetization
of the composite IRMs (Fig. 3) indicates an unblocking temperature
spectra of the soft component at 580◦C, confirming the presence of
magnetite.

### page_4
4 Y.-i. Otofuji et al. / Journal of Geodynamics 91 (2015) 1–12
Fig. 3. Rock magnetic results of selected specimens from Kholchan and Ola vol-
canic suites. The IRM acquisition and thermal demagnetization of three-axes IRMs
imparted by DC fields of 2.0 T, 0.4 T and 0.12 T along three perpendicular axes.
4.2. Paleomagnetism
4.2.1. The NRM intensity
A wide range of initial NRM intensities between 0.05 A/m and
27.4 A/m is observed in the analyzed samples although all of them
are collected from ignimbrite (Fig. 4). Intensities higher than 8
are
A/m
observed in 42 out of 250 samples from sites MA03, MA05,
MA09, MA10, MA12, MA13, MA14 and MA18. However, mean
intensities lower than 5.8 A/m are observed in five of these sites
(MA03, MA10, MA12, MA14 and MA18) and exclusively high inten-
sities are observed in most samples of the other three sites (MA05,
MA09 and MA13). The remaining 72% of the analyzed samples have
intensities ranging between 0.17 A/m and 3.6 A/m.
4.2.2. Demagnetization behavior during ThD and AFD analyses
Demagnetization behavior of the analyzed samples during pro-
gressive ThD depends very much on their NRM intensities. In
general, samples with NRM intensities larger than 5.0 A/m reveal a
single component behavior and a gradual decrease toward the ori-
gin without any visible change in direction (Fig. 5). An unblocking
temperature of approximately 590◦C is observed in such speci-
mens (Fig. 5). Coversely, two components behavior is generally
observed in samples yielding less than 1.7 A/m NRM intensity.
Low and high temperature component magnetizations in the two
components are unblocked at approximately 250◦C and 590◦C,
respectively. Because the characteristic remanent magnetization
(ChRM) is unblocked by 590◦C, magnetite is a main magnetic car-
rier. Two components behavior observed by ThD analyses is also
confirmed by AFD analyses. However, in some samples the AFD
analysis identifies two NRM components where only one compo-
nent is observed by ThD analysis (e.g., site MA05 in Fig. 5 and MA01
in Fig. 6).
Generally, identical NRM directions are observed in most sam-
ples when analyzed either by the ThD or AFD procedures (Fig. 5;
Table 1), however, several samples from site MA01 yield different
directions treated by these procedures (Fig. 6). Two samples from
site MA01 (MA01-1 and MA01-4) with initial NRM intensities over
1.7 A/m reveal a southwestward declination and shallow inclina-
tion prior to demagnetization. Very little change in their directions
appears when analyzed by the ThD procedure. However, signifi-
cant change in direction to northerly declination and steep positive
inclination appears when analyzed by the AFD procedure.
4.2.3. The NRM directions
Because the AFD procedure proved more effective than the ThD
in randomizing the secondary remanent magnetizations, results
from the former procedure are used here to detect the ChRM
directions. The NRM directions are mostly identified by principal
component analysis, however, the great circle method is also used
to determine directional behavior in 11 out of 123 samples. Among
them, two samples are from site MA01 (Fig. 6), seven from site
MA02 and two from site MA09. Because of very strong NRM intensi-
ties (24.9 and 8.6 A/m) two samples of site MA14 are excluded from
final site mean calculations. The results of principal component
analysis and great circle method are listed in Table 1.
The site-mean directions from 16 out of 19 sampling sites reveal
precision parameters (k) larger than 10. Relatively small values of
k (<6.1) appears in the remaining three sites (MA03, MA05 and
MA13) with large NRM intensities (>50 × 10−1A/m) which forced
us to exclude them from the final calculations. Typically larger k
values are observed at sites with lower NRM intensities (Fig. 4b).
However, large k values appeared at two high intensity sites (MA09
and MA14), which could be due to the use of the great circle method
and the exclusion of some very high intensity samples. Accordingly,
16 site-mean directions with k values over 10 are illustrated on
an equal-area projection (Fig. 7a). Following tilt corrections 14 out
of 16 sites yield normal polarity directions with steep downward
inclinations (between 54.5◦and 86.7◦) and the remaining two sites
(MA15 and MA16) reveal reversed polarity directions with steep
upward inclinations (∼−66.2◦). The Late Cretaceous ignimbrites of

the Kholchan and Ola suites thus keep a record of both normal and
reversed polarity directions.
4.2.4. Formation mean direction
As a first option, we calculated formation mean direction on
the basis of 16 site mean directions (Fig. 7a) which yield a mean
direction of D = 43.0◦, I = 76.0◦(˛ =
95
8.1) in geographic coordinates.
Assuming the attitude of eutaxitic texture as a paleohorizontal
plane a tilt-corrected formation mean direction of D = 17.6◦, I = 82.5◦
(˛ =
95
10.6) is calculated. Although both of these directions are
indistinguishable from each other at the 95% confidence limit
(Table 1), relatively large dispersion appears in a tilt-corrected
mean direction (k = 13.1) compared to an in situ mean direction
(k = 21.8). The McElhinny (1964) fold test applied to these data sets
proved inconclusive. However, the correlation test of McFadden
(1990) and the DC tilt test of Enkin (2003) produced negative
results. Bearing in mind a record of both normal and reverse polar-
ities in the studied rocks the negative fold tests may not be due to
remagnetization but rather to inaccurate measurement of the pale-
ohorizontal plane (Lyons et al., 2002). The outcrop-scale eutaxitic
structure, which has been used as a paleohorizontal plane in sev-
eral studies, generally represent an initial dip of flow emplacement
over irregular topography, paleohill slopes or paleostream channels
(McIntosh, 1991; Hagstrum and Gans, 1989; Chapin and Lowell,
1979). However, such outcrop scale structures in ignimbrite cannot
always be used as a true substitute for a large scale paleohorizontal
plane.
Bearing in mind this uncertainty we calculated mean directions
on locality basis as an alternative option (A to F in Fig. 1 and Table 2)
where a unit weight is added to each locality mean before com-
puting an in situ formation mean direction (Dg= 65.6◦, Ig= 75.0◦,
k = 23.3, ˛ =
95
14.2◦, N = 6) and a tilt corrected formation mean direc-
tion (Ds= 42.8◦, Is= 84.7◦, k = 46.0, ˛ =
95
10.0◦, N = 6) (Fig. 7b). These
formation mean directions are shown in Fig. 7b. We adopted this
procedure to randomize an expected error caused by outcrop scale
variations in paleohorizontal features within each locality. This pro-
cedure yields an increase in the k parameter from 23.3 to 46.0
after tilt correction and confirmation of a positive fold test at the
95% confidence limit (McElhinny, 1964). Application of the DC tilt
test (Elkin 2003) to our locality mean direction also produces a
positive test at 78 ± 63% unfolding. As an additional check,
also
we
applied the second definition ((cid:2) )
2
of the McFadden method
(McFadden, 1990; Cogne, 2003) which confirms a positive fold
test at the 95% confidence level. This test reveals a critical value
of 2.862 for parameter (cid:2) c and 3.362 (1.635) for (cid:2) in 2 geographic
coordinates (stratigraphic coordinates). An apparent positive fold
test results from the second option (localities mean direction), and
thus suggests a pre-folding origin for the high-unblocking tem-
perature component in the studied ignimbrites and is accordingly
interpreted as the Late Cretaceous ChRM direction in the Maga-
dan area. Because the Late Cretaceous (86–81 Ma) paleomagnetic
poles calculated here both on the basis of locality-mean (66.7◦N,
168.5◦E, A = 95 18.8◦) and site mean (72.4◦N, 165.7◦E, A = 95 18.9◦)
appear almost identical (Table 3) the earlier one is preferentially
chosen as representative of the Magadan area.
5. Discussion
5.1. Reliability of the NRM directions
As noted above, we used a magnetic compass to orient paleo-
magnetic samples in the field and IGRF declination as a reference for
each sampling site. To check for deflection of magnetic compasses
near high intensity rocks, Gilder et al. (2003) have paleomag-
netically studied basaltic rocks of western Tarim Basin (75◦20(cid:5)E,
40◦17(cid:5)N). For this study rock samples with NRM intensity up to
8 A/m were oriented both with magnetic and sun compasses. Com-
pared to the IGRF declination of 3.9◦ in the study area, an in situ
declination of 3.4 ± 2.3◦was obtained from both types of orienta-
tions This comparison revealed negligible amounts of deflection
in declination due to high (up to 8 A/m) intensity volcanic rocks
and confirmed the reliability of IGRF declination in the study area.
Because 72% of paleomagnetic samples for this study are collected
from ignimbrites with less than 3.6 A/m NRM intensity, their ori-
entations by magnetic compass are considered reliable. At high
latitude the IGRF declination may deflect significantly with respect
to local declination. However, a personal communication from the
Magadan Geophysical Observatory (60.051◦N, 150.728◦E, 226 m)
indicates an average declination of −13.37◦ for 2013, and the
local IGRF shows an average declination of −11.0◦ for the same
period (i.e., no significant error between two sets of orientations).

6 Y.-i. Otofuji et al. / Journal of Geodynamics 91 (2015) 1–12
Fig. 5. In situ vector end-point diagrams for the representative ignimbrite specimens from six localities (A–F) after thermal demagnetization. Solid (open) symbols are
projections onto the horizontal (vertical) plane.
Magnetic compass and IGRF provide an accuracy of orientation at
∼5◦in the Magadan area.
As noted in the results section, samples from three sites (MA03,
MA05 and MA13) which carry NRM intensities higher than 5 A/m
reveal single component behavior during ThD analyses. The site-
mean NRM directions from these sites yield large dispersion
(k < 6.1) compared to the remaining 16 sites. An exceptionally
NRM
high
intensity and excellent directional stability in these sites sug-
gest their complete remagnetization by lightning strike (Dunlop
and Özdemir, 2001), while all other low intensity sites appear to
have been partially remagnetized. As mentioned by Dunlop and
Özdemir (2001), rocks partially remagnetized by lightning strike
could be more successfully demagnetized by AFD procedure com-
pared to ThD. Accordingly, the AFD data from six localities are used

model.
5.2. Poles comparison between the Kolyma-Omolon Composite
Terrane and the Chukotka Terrane
A new Late Cretaceous (86–81 Ma) paleomagnetic pole calcu-
lated for the Magadan area by this study is considered as one of
the representative poles for the Kolyma-Omolon Composite Ter-
rane. Because of its geological juxtaposition with the Chukotka
Terrane, the Late Cretaceous paleomagnetic poles from these ter-
ranes are compared here to discuss a tectonic connection between
them (Fig. 8a).
On the basis of the locality-mean direction from Lake
El’gygytgyn (67◦20(cid:5)N, 172◦00(cid:5)E), Stone et al. (2009) have deter-
mined a Late Cretaceous (90–67 Ma) paleomagnetic pole (69.2◦N,
161.5◦E, A =
95
16.5◦) for the Chukotka Terrane (Fig. 8a). When
compared with the same aged pole from the Kolyma-Omolon Com-
posite Terrane (this study), an angular distance of just 3.6◦ (with
25.0◦ uncertainty at the 95% confidence level) appears between
them. This similarity in pole positions is not unexpected because
the respective data used for these poles come from the OCVB
based igneous rocks which were emplaced on the Kolyma-Omolon
and Chukotka terranes in the Early to Late Cretaceous. An agree-
ment between these two poles, though at a low level of certainty,
indicates no relative tectonic rotation/displacement between the
Kolyma-Omolon and Chukotka terranes since 80 Ma (the time of
OCVB formation). A tectonic model reported by Sokolov et al. (2002,
2009) estimates that a collision between the Kolyma-Omolon Com-
posite Terrane and the Chukotka Terrane along the South Anyui
Suture Zone had ceased by 115–119 Ma. We therefore claim that
the composite Kolyma-Omolon-Chukotka Block behaved as a single
tectonic unit since 80 Ma without any internal deformation. A char-
acteristic 80 Ma paleomagnetic pole of 68.0◦N, 164.7◦E (A =
95
10.9◦,
N = 12) is thus calculated for the Kolyma-Omolon-Chukotka Block

after combining six data sets from the Magadan area (this study)
and six from the Lake El’gygytgyn area (Fig. 8b).
5.3. Comparison between the Eurasian and
Kolyma-Omolon-Chukotka poles
As shown in Fig. 8b, the 80 Ma pole for the composite Kolyma-
Omolon-Chukotka Block is clearly distinguishable from the same
age European and East Asian reference poles. The APWP of Besse
and Courtillot (2002) places the 80 Ma European pole at the 81.4◦N,
206.1◦E (A =
95
5.9◦) position. Using a compilation of paleomagnetic
data from different blocks (including Siberia, Amuria, NCB, SCB and
Korean Peninsula) Cogné et al. (2013) have calculated a new 80 Ma
paleomagnetic pole (79.5◦N, 216.9◦E, A =
95
3.4◦) for East Asia.
When plotted together (Fig. 8b), the 80 Ma poles for Europe and East
Asia fall on similar positions within the 95% confidence limit. How-
ever, the same age pole for the Kolyma-Omolon-Chukotka Block
falls at 16.5–17.5◦south of them.
This southerly pole position of the Kolyma-Omolon-Chukotka
Block with respect to the same age poles from Europe and East
Asia could either be due to changes in geomagnetic field direction
or tectonic movement. Any deviation due to PSV of the geomag-
netic field is discarded here because a reasonable smoothing of this
phenomenon is ascertained by a wide distribution of paleomag-
netic poles in the Kolyma-Omolon-Chukotka Block. In addition,
we deduced an A value
95
of 10.9◦ from 12 locality-based poles
which falls in a reliable range between the A value
95min
of 6.3◦
and the A value
95max
of 17.1◦ (Deenen et al., 2011). A persistent
non-dipolar component of the geomagnetic field can also cause
steepness in inclination and a resultant divergence in pole pos-
itions. However, no such behavior has been observed in the Late
Cretaceous rocks of Eastern Eurasia (Tsuneki et al., 2009; Cogné
et al., 2013). Bearing ithis evidence in mind, we attribute the
pole positions discrepancy between the Kolyma-Omolon-Chukotka
Block and Europe/East Asia to tectonic activity rather than to geo-
magnetic field variations.
5.4. A possible post-80 Ma tectonic scenario of the
Kolyma-Omolon-Chukotka Block
The above mentioned divergence in pole positions suggest that
the composite Kolyma-Omolon-Chukotka Block acted indepen-
dently from the main Eurasian Continent. We thus propose a new
tectonic model in which the main Eurasian Continent is
to
assumed
have experienced an eastward displacement as a result of open-
ing in the Atlantic Ocean, while the Kolyma-Omolon-Chukotka
Block underwent a southward displacement. As a consequence
of these divergent displacements, the Kolyma-Omolon-Chukotka
Block came in to collisional contact with Eurasia.
After assuming an eastward displacement for the main Eurasian
Continent but no displacement for the Kolyma-Omolon-Chukotka
Block since the Cretaceous, an 84 Ma pole of 74.7◦N, 207.7◦E is
calculated for Europe (Fig. 8c). The same age paleopole for main
Eurasia is then reconstructed by rotating it 19.7◦CCW about the
Euler pole 66.5◦N, 148.9◦E (Srivastava et al., 1988; Muller and
Roest, 1992; Gaina et al., 2002). Comparison of the 80 Ma pole
from the Kolyma-Omolon-Chukotka Block with the 84 Ma pole of
main Eurasia reveal an angular distance of 14.8 ± 12.4◦ between
them. This comparison (Fig. 8c) also yields nearly identical pos-
itions for the reconstructed 84 Ma European pole and 80 Ma North
American pole (i.e., 74.7◦N, 207.4◦E, A = 95 5.9◦). However, the
same age pole of the Kolyma-Omolon-Chukotka Block occupied a
divergent position, suggesting a possible southward displacement
(1640 ± 1380 km) of this block with respect to the North American
and main Eurasian blocks.
This estimate of displacement indicates that 80 million years ago
the Kolyma-Omolon-Chukotka Block was located at 75◦N latitude
as a part of the Arctic region. Nearlysimilar paleoposition has been
predicted by some researchers (Lawver et al., 2002; Golonka et al.,
2003; Golonka, 2007; Amato et al., 2004; Drachev and Sunders,
2006) for the Chukotka Terrane in the Early Cretaceous. We ascribe
the post-80 Ma southward displacement of the Kolyma-Omolon-
Chukotka Block to a more than 600 km opening of the Canadian
Basin (Amerasian basin) in the Arctic region. Although several
models have been proposed regarding the Canadian Basin opening
using geological and geophysical observations (Lawver and Scotese,
1990; Lane, 1997; Grantz et al., 1998; Drachev and Sunders, 2006;
Alvey et al., 2008), no clear regional magnetic anomaly pattern is
reported yet for this basin to date the formation of the oceanic crust
(Alvey et al., 2008; Saltus et al., 2011; Pease et al., 2014). The width
of this basin, however, sheds some light on the 1640 ± 1380 km
southward displacement of the Kolyma-Omolon-Chukotka Block
(Fig. 8d).
The predicted southward displacement of the Kolyma-Omolon-
Chukotka Block has probably caused its collision with the Siberian
Craton (a part of the Eurasian Continent) and the ultimate formation
of the peculiar “S” shaped Verkhoyansk and Chersky Ranges. A com-
pressive regime induced by this collision has been documented by

### page_10
10 Y.-i. Otofuji et al. / Journal of Geodynamics 91 (2015) 1–12
Fig. 8. (a) The paleomagnetic poles with 95% confidence circles for the Kolyma-Omolon Composite Terrane (open red star with red circle) and the Chukotka Terrane (triangle
with black circle). These poles are calculated on the basis of locality-mean directions. The paleomagnetic poles calculated from site-mean directions are shown by small
closed circles (red: Kolyma-Omolon Composite Terrane, black: Chukotka Terrane). (b) A paleomagnetic pole with 95% confidence circle for the Kolyma-Omolon-Chukotka
Block (marked as a closed red star with red circle) is compared with the 80 Ma reference poles from Europe (Besse and Courtillot, 2002) and East Asia (Cogné et al., 2013).
The European pole is marked by a dot with blue circle and the East Asian pole by a diamond with black circle. (c) The reconstructed 84 Ma paleoposition of the main Eurasian
Continent is marked by a yellow star. The 80 Ma pole for North America is marked by a pink star. (d) The 80 Ma pole position of the Kolyma-Omolon-Chukotka Block (green
star hemmed by red and a green 95% confidence circle) is located 600 km to north of the present position, assuming that southward displacement of this block is due to
the opening of the Canadian Basin. After 80 Ma, the Kolyma-Omolon-Chukotka Block underwent a southward displacement (green arrow) and the main Eurasian Block
moved eastward (yellow arrow). We predict a collision between the Kolyma-Omolon-Chukotka Block and Eurasia after 80 Ma as a consequence of these displacements. (For
interpretation of the references to color in this figure legend, the reader is referred to the web version of this article.)
several researchers using deformational features in the Verkhoy-
ansk fold-thrust belt (Parfenov, 1991; Sengor and Natalin, 1996;
Layer et al., 2001; Oxman, 2003; Prokopiev and Oxman, 2009). In
addition to this, on the basis of vitrinite reflectance analysis it has
been suggested (Parfenov et al., 1995) that structural shortening in
the Verkhoyansk fold-thrust belt started in the Early Jurassic and
ended in the Late Cretaceous.
The post-80 Ma southward displacement of the Kolyma-
Omolon-Chukotka Block predicted by this study, however, faces
some contradiction with the reported geological interpretation. A
geological constraint (Khanchuk et al., 2006) which goes against
this displacement is the extent of OCVB in the Kolyma-Omolon-
Chukotka Block and an overlay of its extreme western margin on the
Siberian Craton. This problem is, however, overcome by the Early
Cretaceous (142–120 Ma) paleomagnetic results reported from the
Verkhoyansk depression of the Siberian Platform (Metelkin et
2008)
al.,
which yields a pole position of 67.2◦N, 183.8◦E (A =
95
7.8◦)
and a resultant southward displacement of 500 km for this block
compared to the same age poles from Europe. Comparison of this
Siberian pole with the one determined for the Kolyma-Omolon-
Chukotka Block (this study) yields a southward displacement of
both of these terranes which solves the above noted problem
regarding a geological contact between the OCVB and the Siberian
platform. Nevertheless, we recommend the collection of additional
geological, geo-chronological and paleomagnetic data from the
OCVB to overcome any unclear issues regarding the post-80 Ma
southward displacement of the Kolyma-Omolon-Chukotka Block.
6. Conclusions
Based on the new paleomagnetic results from the 86–81 Ma old
ignimbrites of the Magadan area (the Kolyma-Omolon Composite

### page_11
Y.-i. Otofuji et al. / Journal of Geodynamics 91 (2015) 1–12 11
Terrane) we suggest the following conclusions about the northeast
Eurasian tectonics.
(1) After successfully eliminating a lightning induced secondary
magnetization by AFD procedure, the Late Cretaceous charac-
teristic mean direction (D = 42.8◦, I = 84.7◦, k = 46.0, ˛ =
95
10.0◦)
with a corresponding pole of 66.7◦N, 168.5◦E (A = 95 18.8◦) is
estimated for the Magadan area.
(2) This new pole falls on the 67–90 Ma pole reported from Lake
El’gygytgyn (Chukotka Terrane), revealing that the Kolyma-
Omolon Composite Terrane and the Chukotka Terrane behaved
as a single tectonic unit since 80 Ma. Accordingly a combined
80 Ma pole (68.0◦, 164.7◦E, A =
95
10.9◦) is calculated for the
Kolyma-Omolon-Chukotka Block.
(3) This combined pole from 12 localities falls at 16.5–17.5◦
south of the coeval Eurasian poles, yielding a southward dis-
placement of more than 260 km (1640 ± 1380 km) for the
Kolyma-Omolon-Chukotka Block with respect to the main
Eurasian and North American continents.
(4) Such large scale displacement of the Kolyma-Omolon-Chukotka
Block could be ascribed to a post-80 Ma opening of the Canadian
Basin in the Arctic Ocean.
